title: the summit sit
hook: namah, namah, namah: a hymn that faces an angry god with a strung bow, and starts by bowing

segments.voice: Yesterday, the summit sit stood in front of Nataraja and read him all at once: the drum and the flame, held level. Did you notice something beginning just as something ended? Day one thousand four hundred fifteen.
screen: `THE SUMMIT SIT.` · `THE DRUM AND THE FLAME, LEVEL.`

segments.voice: Namah. Namah. Namah. Said once, it's a bow, a word of homage. Said over and over, in a steady chant, it becomes a rhythm you can feel in the floor. The hymn that's built on it faces a god who is not, at first, gentle. Rudra stands with his bow strung and an arrow ready. And the hymn doesn't run, and doesn't argue. It bows. To the arrow. To the bow. To the anger itself. Today's summit sit climbs back to the Rudram, and the night the year spent awake with Shiva.
screen: `NAMAH, NAMAH, NAMAH.` → `A GOD WITH A STRUNG BOW.` → `THE HYMN BOWS.`

segments.voice: The Rudram comes from the Yajur Veda. It opens, in paraphrase, by bowing to Rudra's anger, and to his arrow, and to his arms. Then it asks: make that arrow gentle. Let the form of you that is kind be turned toward us. That's the first move. Fear isn't hidden or argued away. It's bowed to, and asked to soften. Then the hymn widens. It bows to Rudra in the short and the tall, the eldest and the youngest. In the trees with green hair. In the rain and in the drought, in the well and in the foam on the water. In thieves, even, and in the carpenters and the potters. Line after line, namah, until almost nothing in the world has been left out of the bowing. Rudra isn't only on the mountain. He's in the crowd, and the weather, and the workshop. Then comes its companion, often chanted right after it, and the direction turns. Line after line, it asks, and to me: strength, food, breath, peace, long life. Bowing to everything, then asking honestly for what a person needs. And the year carried that hymn into the dark, too. On Maha Shivaratri, it's chanted while water pours over the linga, through a night kept awake, often without food, until the gray light comes. From up here, the shape of the whole Shiva stretch is clearer. A god who frightens, faced by a hymn that bows. A bowing so wide it takes in the potter and the thief. And a long night where the only thing to do is stay awake and keep bowing.
screen: `BOW TO THE ANGER. ASK THE ARROW TO SOFTEN.` · `NAMAH TO THE TREES, THE RAIN, THE POTTER.` · `AND TO ME: AN HONEST ASK.` · `A NIGHT KEPT AWAKE.` · then, large: `NOTHING LEFT OUT OF THE BOWING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a wide bow. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then let the bowing move outward, slowly, one thing per breath. Bow, inwardly, to your own body, sitting here. To the room. To the people in the building or on the street. To the weather outside. To someone who makes you angry. If something feels too hard to bow to, notice that, and bow to the hard feeling instead. If you pray, you can say namah, softly, with each one. The bell holds the time.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: the Rudram and Shivaratri, a hymn that bows to an angry god and then to everything. Today's word.

Your line: the summit sit. Today, when something frightens or angers you, try the Rudram's first move: don't fight it at once. Name it, give it a small bow inside, and ask it to soften. Day one thousand four hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: The Sri Rudram is chanted in Shiva temples and homes, often during abhisheka, when water, milk or other offerings are poured over the linga, and through the night of Maha Shivaratri.

fork.setup: you're facing Rudra. his bow is strung and the arrow is ready. what does the hymn do first?
options: call on another god for protection.
bow to his anger and ask the arrow to be gentle.
list the reasons he shouldn't be angry.
fork.reveal: the Rudram bows to the anger, the arrow and the bow, then asks that the kind form of Rudra be turned toward us. fear is bowed to, not argued away.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: namaḥ, a bow, homage, the word the Rudram repeats until it becomes the rhythm.

trapdoor: what you thought: namah is a polite word, like hello.
what it means: in the Rudram it's a bow, said again and again, to Rudra in everything.
what a scholar hears: the Shatarudriya of the Taittiriya Samhita, bowing to Rudra's anger, followed by the Chamakam with its repeated ca me, and to me.
